name: Rosa Tanaka

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Whatever you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. To begin, describe an ordinary working day.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I buy fresh produce and imported specialty foods for a distributor that supplies about four hundred restaurants and hotel kitchens. My day starts at five with the market reports and a call to the growers in the south, because weather decides everything. By nine I'm setting prices and quantities for the next week, and by afternoon I'm talking a chef out of panic over a missing delivery of figs. I love it. What wears me out is that one spoiled pallet is my mistake in everyone's eyes, even when a strike at the port caused it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say good, a few boring jobs get easier and we can spend more time with the growers. To friends I'd say it's typical, big promises and small results. Online I'd probably keep quiet, since I don't want to argue with people who think the end is near.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd feel calm, because my job is built on relationships and judgement that don't change in a quiet world. The pressure I carry has nothing to do with AI, it's margins. The big supermarket chains squeeze our prices, and my bonus depends on a year that's already tough.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on and keep trying the forecast tool once a week, since it saves me an hour on the price sheet. I'd keep the savings plan, a bit more each month, and finish my last two years of building a buffer so retirement feels less thin. I'd take my holiday with Kenji in spring and not feel guilty.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels settled, honestly. A little dull, a little relieved. I like a world where my experience keeps its value.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd be fine. What would still keep you up at night in that picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Margins and the chains. If a big retailer drops us for a cheaper distributor, my team goes first and I'm left explaining it. That's the thing that wakes me up, not a robot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd keep using the forecast tool. How do you decide when to trust it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I look at what it said last week against what actually happened. If it's right four weeks out of five I lean on it, and if a price moves in a way I don't understand, I pick up the phone to a grower. It's a second opinion, not my boss.

say: At work I'd say a few **boring jobs** get easier and we can focus on growers.
To friends I'd say it's **big promises, small results**.
think: My **judgement and relationships** keep their value, so I feel calm about the job.
My real pressure is **retailer margins**, which squeeze our prices and could cost my team its work.
do: Keep using the **forecast tool** weekly to save an hour on the price sheet.
Add a little more each month to the **retirement buffer**.
feel: **Settled** and slightly relieved, with a dull edge.
S0.quote: The pressure I carry has nothing to do with AI, it's margins.
fieldNote: She is **calm** because her work rests on relationships, and her pressure is margins from big chains.
She treats the tool as a **second opinion**, checking it against what happens, which shows a steady, evidence-led style.

steps.text: Use the price forecast tool once a week and check it
Add a bit more to savings each month
Keep the growers' weekly calls and relationships going

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the next picture, called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's real and we need to be honest with staff. At work I'd ask management to put in writing which tasks go to software and which jobs are protected. I'd say it to friends too: the gains should be shared, not just banked.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, a lot of my day is exactly the thinking work on that card: checking quotes, planning quantities, rebooking. Software can do the routine half. So the team gets smaller, there are fewer junior buyers, and the question is whether my experience stays valued.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd become the person who understands the tool, learn it properly over the next few months, and make sure I'm the one choosing which parts we automate. I'd also train the juniors on the relationship side, since the software can't do that. And I'd move my savings plan up, say 400 a month, in case it goes the wrong way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. My own job looks safe for now, but the people around me are in danger, and I feel responsible for them. It's like watching the tide come in on someone else's beach.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said your team would feel it. Which part of the buying would software take first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Re-ordering and quote-checking, first. The software already suggests the order and I've been editing it for a year. In another year or two it'll just place it and I'll check the exceptions.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want the company to promise you in that world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No compulsory redundancies for the junior team without a retraining offer, and a say when the tools come in. I'd go to the staff forum and the union branch and push for it. If we get that, I can be positive.

say: I'd ask management to **put in writing** which tasks go to software.
I'd say the **gains should be shared**, not just banked.
think: Much of my day is **thinking work**, so the junior buyer roles will shrink first.
My own job looks safe, but I'm **worried for my team** and for my own long-term value.
do: Learn the tools **properly** and choose which parts to automate.
Train the juniors on **supplier relationships** the software can't do.
feel: **Uneasy**, responsible for colleagues more than for myself.
S1.quote: No compulsory redundancies for the junior team without a retraining offer, and a say when the tools come in.
fieldNote: Her worry is **mostly for her team**, and she turns it into practical demands on management.
She chooses to **lead the adoption** rather than resist it, which fits her steady, proof-first attitude.

steps.text: Learn the buying tool properly and pick what to automate
Train junior buyers on grower and chef relationships
Push the staff forum for a retraining-first rule

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the next picture, called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is a shock, and it can't be left to the market. I'd call for emergency rules on notice periods, income support and retraining. I'd say it publicly, and I'd say it to my CEO, since someone has to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us I think my job is gone or nearly gone by 2028. Buying is a thinking job and AI does it better and faster. The robots come three years later and they'd move the warehouse and the trucks. That's the part where my firm may stop needing most of us at all.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First week, I'd sit down with Kenji and do the real numbers. I'd cut what we can, the holiday and the new kitchen. I'd ask my boss for a plan, and if there isn't one, I'd start looking at consulting for small food makers who can't afford a buyer. I'd also join the union branch and push for a bridge scheme.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. It's a physical thing, a heavy feeling in the chest. I keep thinking of the sums: three months of savings against four or five years before we can both stop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Two years. What would you do in your first week?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd talk plainly, which we are good at. His job is safer, nurses will be needed for a long time, and he could take extra shifts. I'd be the one to retrain or find new work, and we'd go down to one comfortable income if we must.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said both you and Kenji might be hit. How would you handle that between the two of you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably cut my pension contributions for a while if things were bad, which scares me. I'd want my employer to let me keep the contributions flowing through a notice period. That's the sort of rule I'd push for.

say: I'd call for **emergency rules** on notice, income support and retraining.
I'd say it **publicly** and to my CEO.
think: I expect my buying job to be **done by AI** by 2028, and the warehouse robots to follow.
The sums frighten me: **three months saved** against several years to go.
do: Sit down with Kenji and do the **real numbers**.
Cut the **holiday** and the new kitchen.
Look at **consulting** for small food makers who can't afford a buyer.
feel: **Alarmed**, with a heavy feeling in the chest.
S2.quote: I keep thinking of the sums: three months of savings against four or five years before we can both stop.
fieldNote: She is **alarmed but organised**, moving straight to numbers and a consulting idea.
The couple's **different exposure** (her desk job, his nursing) shapes a calm, shared plan.

steps.text: Sit down with Kenji and cut the holiday and new kitchen
Offer consulting to small food makers who can't hire a buyer
Join the union branch and push for a bridge scheme
Ask the boss for a written plan for the buying team

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the next picture, called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we have a window and we must use it. Pass the rules now, fund the retraining, make companies pay in. I'd say it loudly, but without panic, because a calm, serious plan sells better.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, it's still scary, since I'd be 63 and I'd have only one or two working years left once it lands. The extra time lets me finish the buffer and decide what I want, which is better than two years. But the end point is the same.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd spend the first two years finishing a six-month savings buffer and building the consulting idea on the side, with two or three small food makers as test clients. I'd learn the tools well enough to explain them to others. In year four or five I'd decide, in a calm way, whether to go to part-time or retire.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but I have a plan, so it doesn't feel paralysing. Five years is the difference between being late for a flight and having time to pack.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Five years is better than two. What exactly does it let you do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably nothing formal. A short course in running a small advisory business, and the AI tools for forecasting that I'd use on myself. At my age I'm not going to start a degree.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd retrain. What would you actually study?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd try to carry on as a buyer for as long as the firm wants me, using the extra years to build the second income so that when the main one stops, it doesn't all stop at once.

say: I'd say we have a **window** and should pass rules and fund retraining now.
I'd say it **loudly but calmly**, since a serious plan persuades more.
think: Even with five years I'd be **63 at the end**, with only a couple of working years left.
The extra time lets me **finish my buffer** and test a second income.
do: Build a **six-month savings** buffer over two years.
Test the **consulting idea** with two or three small food makers.
Decide in year five between **part-time and retiring**.
feel: **Anxious**, but with a plan so it isn't paralysing.
S3.quote: Five years is the difference between being late for a flight and having time to pack.
fieldNote: She uses the extra time **build a second income**, not to retrain formally.
Her anxiety is **softened** by having a plan, which fits her steady, proof-first attitude.

steps.text: Build a six-month savings buffer within two years
Test consulting with three small food makers on the side
Learn the forecasting tools well enough to teach others
Choose between part-time and retirement in year five

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the next picture, called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a long enough runway to do this properly, but only if people take it seriously now. Public money for retraining, tax on the firms that gain. I'd say we shouldn't let ten years make us lazy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us I'd be 68, retired for years already, so it's not my fight in the same way. I'd feel guilty for how relaxed I am. My worry is for the younger buyers and for the food industry I love.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd work until about 62, retire on schedule, and spend part of retirement volunteering with a food bank that runs a training kitchen. Meanwhile I'd keep using the tools and teach the young buyers how to question the output.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fairly calm for myself, a little uneasy overall. I like having a long timeline, because I can do some good with it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Ten years is a long time. What would you do differently from the other two?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: To learn the relationship side of buying, to be curious about the tools but not dependent on them, and to build savings early. I'd also tell them to find a union or association that fits them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell younger buyers in your team?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably help set up a mentoring scheme at my firm, so juniors learn from retiring buyers before we go. If we use the ten years well, they'll be in a better spot than I would have been.

say: I'd say ten years is **enough runway** only if people act now.
I'd call for **public money** for retraining and a fair tax on firms that gain.
think: I'd be **retired for years** by then, so I feel almost guilty for being relaxed.
My real worry is the **younger buyers** and the food industry I love.
do: Work until about **62** and retire on schedule.
Volunteer with a **food bank** that runs a training kitchen.
Set up a **mentoring scheme** pairing juniors with retiring buyers.
feel: **Fairly calm** for myself, a little uneasy overall.
S4.quote: I'd probably help set up a mentoring scheme at my firm, so juniors learn from retiring buyers before we go.
fieldNote: With ten years her worry **shifts** from herself to the juniors, and she sees her role as a mentor.
She admits **guilt** at her own calm, which is a candid and human touch.

steps.text: Set up a mentoring scheme pairing juniors with retiring buyers
Volunteer with a food bank training kitchen

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one worries me most. I'm 58, I have about three months' savings, and Kenji, my partner, is a nurse with two years to go, so we can't both stumble at once. What would help is rules about notice and retraining paid for by the companies that profit, plus a public safety net that actually pays. I'd also want some say at my own firm in how the tools come in.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: I'd only say that the people who made these decisions should sit in the room with the workers affected, not just the owners and the engineers. I'm already using them for price forecasts. I'll learn any tool they put in front of me, but I won't be told it's fine by people who won't be the ones losing a job.

headlineQuote: I'll learn any tool they put in front of me, but I won't be told it's fine by people who won't be the ones losing a job.
portrait: **Rosa** is 58, a senior buyer of fresh produce and specialty foods for a distributor serving restaurants and hotels.
She is **open to proven change**, uses AI for price forecasts now and then, and wants to see results first.
Progressive in outlook, she backs **regulation and public support**, and blames big retailers and lax rules more than the technology.
With about **three months saved** and a nurse partner two years from retiring, she can't afford a stumble.
She moves from steady to **alarmed** as the warning time shrinks, and wants notice, paid retraining and a voice.
biggestWorry: The **2028 picture** worries her most, because both she and her partner would be close to retirement with thin savings.
whatWouldHelp: She wants **paid retraining** funded by firms that profit, a real safety net, and a voice in how tools arrive.
